title: The hypertrophy series: modifying sessions frequency to control volume/intensity
summary: NH introduces frequency as the third pillar of programming alongside volume and intensity. Frequency exists both within a workout and between sessions, rising complexity suits only advanced lifters, and poor frequency silently kills gains by undermining recovery.
claims: Frequency is a pillar of programming and must be mastered with volume and intensity to control tonnage
Frequency exists on two planes: within a workout (sets and reps on a body part) and between sessions across the week
Monday's volume on a muscle dictates when you can train it again that week
He runs an 8-day program cycle, training 6 days and resting 1, so a full cycle takes 9 days
All his rep ranges are evolving, adding complexity
Novices need low frequency and low complexity: about 3 days a week, no lift rotations
As you advance, complexity must rise to keep effectiveness, and well-designed complexity adds flexibility
Poor volume or intensity can be survived, but poor frequency silently kills gains by robbing recovery
Training again before full recovery steals gains from previous sessions
Frequency is about how much time you need between sessions to train hard every time; you must discover your own recovery
Lower body lifts are generally more taxing, but whether squat or deadlift tires you more varies, so deadlift frequency may be higher than squat frequency
Some find 3x a week horizontal pressing too much for their shoulders, despite being a good progress frequency
Tonnage sits above volume and intensity; frequency is not directly linked to tonnage
